units.title: Lines
units.blurb: Straight and curved, standing and leaning, zigzag and wavy, thick and thin: the lines every drawing is made of.

units.title: Shapes
units.blurb: Circles, squares, triangles and their friends, and the free shapes of clouds and leaves.

units.title: Drawing from Shapes
units.blurb: Houses, cats, fish, birds, cars, trees and flowers, built one shape at a time.

units.title: Colors
units.blurb: The rainbow, the primary colors, mixing new colors, warm and cool, lighter and darker, and the color wheel.

units.title: Patterns and Mirror Halves
units.blurb: Patterns that repeat, what comes next, patterns on animals and plants, and symmetry.

units.title: Faces, Feelings and People
units.blurb: Where the parts of a face go, how a face shows feelings, and people built from shapes.

units.title: Using the Whole Page
units.blurb: Drawing big, sky and ground, and near and far.

units.title: Looking Closely
units.blurb: Drawing what you see, counting details, showing how things feel, and where shadows fall.

units.title: Artists and Their Tools
units.blurb: Crayons, paint and clay; portraits, landscapes and still lifes; flat pictures and solid sculptures.

topics.title: Straight and Curved Lines
topics.short: A straight line goes one way without bending. A curved line bends, like a smile or a rainbow.
topics.trouble: Children call a neat line "straight" and a slightly wobbly straight line "curved." The question to ask is whether the line bends on purpose.

topics.title: Lines That Stand, Lie and Lean
topics.short: A vertical line stands up tall, a horizontal line lies down flat, and a diagonal line leans.
topics.trouble: Children mix up "vertical" and "horizontal." Tie the words to the body: standing up tall is vertical; lying down flat, like the horizon, is horizontal.

topics.title: Zigzag, Wavy and Spiral Lines
topics.short: A zigzag line has sharp points, a wavy line has smooth bumps, and a spiral winds around and around.
topics.trouble: Children mix up zigzag and wavy lines because both go up and down. A zigzag has sharp corners; a wave is smooth all the way.

topics.title: Thick and Thin, Light and Dark
topics.short: Press gently for a thin, light line. Press harder, or use a fatter tool, for a thick, dark line.
topics.trouble: Children press hard on every line, so every line looks the same and nothing erases. Starting light lets you change your mind.

topics.title: Lines All Around Us
topics.short: Lines are everywhere: stripes on a zebra, rungs on a ladder, waves on the water. Artists notice them and draw them.
topics.trouble: Children look for lines only in drawings. Real things have lines too: edges, stripes, cracks and the folds in a shirt.

topics.title: Circle, Square and Triangle
topics.short: A circle is round with no corners. A square has four equal sides and four corners. A triangle has three sides and three corners.
topics.trouble: Children call a square turned on its corner a "diamond" and think it is a new shape. Turning a shape does not change it.

topics.title: Rectangles, Ovals and More
topics.short: A rectangle is a stretched square, an oval is a stretched circle, and hearts, stars and diamonds are shapes too.
topics.trouble: Children call every four-sided shape a square. A rectangle has two long sides and two short sides.

topics.title: Finding Shapes in Things
topics.short: Look at a thing and find its shapes: a wheel is a circle, a door is a rectangle, a roof is a triangle.
topics.trouble: Children draw the idea of a thing instead of the shapes they see. Naming the shapes first makes the drawing easier.

topics.title: Neat Shapes and Free Shapes
topics.short: Shapes with straight sides and even curves are geometric. Free, bumpy shapes like leaves, clouds and puddles are organic.
topics.trouble: Children think a shape needs a name to count as a shape. A cloud or a puddle is a shape too: a free, organic one.

topics.title: Draw a House from Shapes
topics.short: A square or rectangle for the walls, a triangle for the roof, and small rectangles for the door and windows.
topics.trouble: Children start with the small things, like a doorknob, and run out of room. Big shapes first, details last.

topics.title: Draw a Cat from Shapes
topics.short: A circle for the head, two triangles for the ears, an oval for the body, and a curved line for the tail.
topics.trouble: Children draw the head and body the same size. A cat's body is bigger than its head.

topics.title: Draw a Fish and a Bird
topics.short: An oval and a triangle make a fish. An oval body, a circle head, a triangle beak and a curved wing make a bird.
topics.trouble: Children put a fish's tail fin on the head end. The tail triangle goes on the back end, pointing out.

topics.title: Draw a Car or a Train
topics.short: Rectangles for the body and windows and circles for the wheels. The wheels touch the road.
topics.trouble: Children float the wheels inside the car or below the road. Wheels sit at the bottom edge and touch the ground.

topics.title: Draw Trees and Flowers
topics.short: A tall rectangle trunk and a cloud shape for leaves; a circle center with petals around it for a flower.
topics.trouble: Children draw petals of every size on one side only. Petals go all the way around the center, about the same size.

topics.title: In Front and Behind
topics.short: When one thing is in front of another, draw the front one whole. The one behind is partly hidden.
topics.trouble: Children draw every shape whole, so a thing behind looks see-through. Stop the back shape's line where the front shape begins.

topics.title: The Colors of the Rainbow
topics.short: A rainbow always shows its colors in the same order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet.
topics.trouble: Children put the rainbow's colors in any order. The order never changes: red on the outside edge, violet on the inside.

topics.title: The Primary Colors
topics.short: In paint, red, yellow and blue are the primary colors. Many other colors can be mixed from them.
topics.trouble: Children think green is a primary color in paint. Green paint can be mixed from yellow and blue.

topics.title: Mixing New Colors
topics.short: Mix two primary colors to make a secondary color: red and yellow make orange, yellow and blue make green, red and blue make purple.
topics.trouble: Children stir every color together and get brown. Mix only two colors at a time, and clean the brush between colors.

topics.title: Warm and Cool Colors
topics.short: Red, orange and yellow look warm, like fire and the sun. Blue, green and purple look cool, like water and leaves.
topics.trouble: Children sort colors by the ones they like best. Warm and cool are about fire and sun versus water, sky and leaves, not favorites.

topics.title: Lighter and Darker Colors
topics.short: Add white to make a color lighter. Add a tiny bit of black to make it darker.
topics.trouble: Children add a big blob of black and the color turns almost black. Add dark colors a tiny bit at a time.

topics.title: The Color Wheel
topics.short: A color wheel puts the colors in a circle. Colors across from each other, like red and green, are opposites, and they make each other look bright.
topics.trouble: Children think opposite colors "don't go together." Opposites side by side look bright and lively; that is why artists use them.

topics.title: Patterns That Repeat
topics.short: A pattern repeats the same part again and again: red, blue, red, blue.
topics.trouble: Children repeat the part once and then change the rule. Say the pattern aloud to keep it going.

topics.title: What Comes Next?
topics.short: Find the part that repeats, then use it to tell what comes next.
topics.trouble: Children guess from the last thing only. Look for the whole part that repeats, like circle, circle, star.

topics.title: Patterns in Nature
topics.short: Stripes, spots, scales and spirals are patterns on animals and plants.
topics.trouble: Children think only people make patterns. Zebras, snails, pinecones and fish have patterns too.

topics.title: Mirror Halves
topics.short: A thing is symmetrical when one half is a mirror picture of the other half, like a butterfly.
topics.trouble: Children copy the half instead of flipping it, so the two sides point the same way. A mirror half faces the other way.

topics.title: Where the Face Parts Go
topics.short: The eyes go about halfway down the head. The nose sits below the eyes, and the mouth below the nose.
topics.trouble: Children put the eyes near the top of the head, with no room for a forehead. The eyes are about halfway down.

topics.title: Happy, Sad and Surprised
topics.short: A mouth that curves up looks happy. A mouth that curves down looks sad. A round open mouth looks surprised.
topics.trouble: Children draw every face with the same smile. The shape of the mouth changes with the feeling.

topics.title: Eyebrows Show Feelings
topics.short: Eyebrows raised high look surprised. Eyebrows that slope down toward the nose look cross.
topics.trouble: Children change only the mouth. Eyebrows tell as much about a feeling as the mouth does.

topics.title: People from Shapes
topics.short: Build a person from shapes: an oval head, a body, and long shapes for arms and legs. Then add clothes.
topics.trouble: Children attach the arms to the head. Arms start at the shoulders, at the top of the body.

topics.title: Hair, Hats and Clothes
topics.short: Make each person different with hair, hats, glasses and clothes.
topics.trouble: Children draw everyone the same. Changing hair, clothes, size and glasses shows who is who.

topics.title: Draw It Big
topics.short: Make the main thing big enough to fill the page, not tiny in a corner.
topics.trouble: Children draw a tiny picture in one corner and leave the page empty. Touching the edges with the big shapes is fine.

topics.title: Sky and Ground
topics.short: Put the ground along the bottom and the sky above it. The sky comes all the way down to the land.
topics.trouble: Children paint a thin strip of blue at the very top, with white air between the sky and the ground. The sky reaches down to where the land ends.

topics.title: Near and Far
topics.short: Things far away look smaller and sit higher on the page. Near things look bigger and sit lower.
topics.trouble: Children draw a faraway tree as big as a near one. Far things look smaller.

topics.title: Draw What You See
topics.short: Look at the real thing more than at your paper. Notice its shapes before you draw them.
topics.trouble: Children draw a lollipop tree from memory instead of the tree in front of them. Looking often is the trick.

topics.title: Counting the Details
topics.short: Count the legs, petals or windows before you draw, so your drawing has the right number.
topics.trouble: Children guess the number: a spider with six legs, a hand with seven fingers. Count first.

topics.title: Bumpy, Smooth and Fuzzy
topics.short: Different marks show how things feel: short lines for fur, dots for sand, long smooth lines for water.
topics.trouble: Children color everything the same flat way. The kind of mark you make can show fur, bark or sand.

topics.title: Light and Shadow
topics.short: A shadow falls on the side away from the light.
topics.trouble: Children put the shadow on the same side as the sun. The shadow points away from the light.

topics.title: An Artist's Tools
topics.short: Crayons, pencils, markers, paint and brushes, clay and scissors each make a different kind of art.
topics.trouble: Children think art means only crayons and paper. Clay, paper cutouts and paint are art tools too.

topics.title: Portraits, Landscapes and Still Lifes
topics.short: A portrait shows a person. A landscape shows land and sky. A still life shows things on a table.
topics.trouble: Children call any picture with a person in it a portrait. A portrait is about the person; a big outdoor scene with tiny people is a landscape.

topics.title: Pictures and Sculptures
topics.short: A painting or a drawing is flat. A sculpture is solid: you can walk around it.
topics.trouble: Children think a sculpture must be a statue of a person. A clay bowl, a carved animal and a tall metal shape are sculptures too.
